analysis.body:
# US Grid Interconnection Queues: September 2026

Across the five major US grid operators tracked here—ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO—there are 8,379 pending generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million megawatts waiting to connect to the grid as of mid-September 2026. While these queues measure planned infrastructure rather than data center demand directly, they reflect the power supply race underway in regions where large digital loads cluster. Texas leads by far with ERCOT's 438,086 MW in queue, followed by NYISO at 319,115 MW in New York, then MISO at 299,721 MW across the Midwest and upper South. Storage projects—which now account for 326,700 MW across all queues—and natural gas capacity growth (totaling 184,345 MW) are two reliable indicators that grid planners are bracing for sustained high demand, since neither storage nor gas plants are typically overbuilt.

Commercial-sector electricity sales across eight major data center hub states reached 54,798 megawatt-hours in June 2026, with Texas consuming 15,754 MWh at the cheapest rate of $8.66 per MWh, while California consumed 10,025 MWh at $27.33 per MWh—a threefold price gap that reflects both grid stress and generation mix. Virginia, Georgia, and Ohio—all emerging AI infrastructure regions—together accounted for 18,906 MWh of the eight-state total. These commercial sales volumes are a proxy for data center load rather than a direct measurement, since data centers occupy the commercial billing class alongside office buildings and retail; the June-to-September lag in this data means current demand is likely already higher.

Solar and wind dominate the generation-side queue (totaling 533,760 MW) but appear mismatched to data center timing needs, since these intermittent sources require storage or gas peaking support to serve continuous loads. ERCOT's queue is weighted 34 percent solar and 11 percent wind, while MISO leans 49 percent solar and 17 percent wind; both depend heavily on the storage projects also in their queues to firm up supply. Watch whether storage capacity in Texas and California queues begins commissioning faster than solar, since that will signal whether grid operators expect data center demand to arrive before the solar buildout can support it.
